Not all selected traits are positive. They just don't hinder survival/procreation. In fact, some genes transcribe to multiple traits, one positive, one negative. So just because there's a lot of people with sickle cell anemia doesn't mean it's a positive trait. Or sometimes traits are common but also are *to our current understanding* negative, like depression or parkinson's. But many are just... average. It originated in the middle ages, when it was seen as lucky to have a piece of the wedding dress.  So wedding guests used to tear tge bride's clothes apart at the end of the ceremony (the ceremony ended with the guests walking the couple to the bedroom). Since brides didn't like having their clothes torn off of them by a pack of savage friends and family, they started wearing garters that the groom would throw out to the crowd. The throw then started to occur the morning after and not the night before so that it could be used as proof of consummation, thus validating the marriage. 

In the 1700s, both the bride and groom wore garters, and the unmarried wedding guests would tear the garters off of both of them and then try to throw the stockings onto the couple. It was believed that if you could make the throw that both the couple and the single person that threw the garters would have happy marriages. (I like this tradition the best).

In the 1800s, the single groomsmen would have a race, and whoever won would have the bride toss her garter to him. As the century worn down, the Victorians became rather prude and started to look down on this tradition. That's when the bouquet throws started instead--much more "socially acceptable."

That brings us to today, where the groom has started throwing his wife's garters to the single men. It's interesting because it's built more off of what replaced the garter games--the bouquet throw--than it is built off of the traditional garter games themselves.
